items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: I had seen Sissle on stage when I was in Cincinnati... I was never a lover of the soprano sax so Bechet didn't tell me anything... I felt sorry for the musicians because they had no leader that knew beans about jazz.

ctx.x: Russel was now employing three trumpets and Higginbotham was not there. The line-up was Jimmy Archey, trombone, Henry 'Moon' Jones had replaced Charlie Holmes on alto sax, Greely Walton had replaced Teddy Hill on tenor-sax, Albert Nicholas, alto-sax and clarinet, Bill Johnson, guitar, Paul Barbarin, drums, Pops Foster, bass, Bill Dillard, Red Allen and myself, trumpets. And this time I had more solos and played some of the first parts also.

One night the orchestra of Noble Sissle who was working in a big white hotel was engaged at the Arcadia to play a battle of jazz between Russell and the other white orchestra whose name I don't remember. I had seen Sissle on stage when I was in Cincinnati and in my estimation he was pretty much a ham actor. So it was a night that we were looking forward to, and the Uncle Tom in him was really shown when his band came in dressed in red frocktail coats which made them look like a circus monkey band. There were some…

trombonist and Sidney Bechet who was supposed to be the jazz man of the band, but I was never a lover of the soprano sax so Bechet didn't tell me anything. The band as a whole was the most jazzless negro orchestra I had ever heard. The white band made Sissle's sound like a fifth-grade school band and Russel's orchestra made Sissles sound like it was the first time they had ever played musical instruments.
